snippet.title: The Day Molasses Flooded Boston
snippet.description:
When the molasses wave hit Boston’s North End, Martin Clougherty was asleep at home. He woke beneath the wreckage, found his sister Teresa, and tried to reach their mother.

The disaster began with a leaking tank that remained in use. When its walls burst on January 15, 1919, molasses swept through the streets, tore homes from their foundations, and damaged the elevated railway. Martin survived, but his search for Bridget ended with devastating news. The flood killed 21 people and injured around 150.

Years later, the court rejected the company’s claim that a bomb had destroyed the tank. The case found construction flaws, negligence and poor management, and held the company responsible. This film tells the Boston Molasses Flood through the people caught in it and the decisions that preceded it.

snippet.title: Why Claude Waited While ChatGPT Took Off #ClaudeAI #ChatGPT
snippet.description:
Before ChatGPT became a sensation, the team building its future rival made a different choice: wait.

Dario Amodei had worked on AI at OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic. As his team developed Claude, they worried that a rush to release powerful AI could leave too little time to make it safe.

OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022. Anthropic introduced Claude the following March. Years later, Amodei said the delay had probably cost Anthropic its chance to lead in AI for everyday users.

snippet.title: A Giant Freighter Vanished. No Distress Call Was Heard.
snippet.description:
In November 1975, the Edmund Fitzgerald crossed Lake Superior as a severe storm intensified around the freighter.

The Edmund Fitzgerald left Superior on November 9, 1975, bound for the Detroit area with 29 people aboard and more than 26,000 tons of iron ore. The 200-meter freighter was making another crossing of the Great Lakes when a powerful storm closed in on Lake Superior.

The Fitzgerald and the Arthur M. Anderson changed course toward the Canadian shore, then tried to reach the more protected waters of Whitefish Bay. The Fitzgerald reported damage, a list and pumps running. Later its radars failed, and the Anderson helped by radio with the ship’s position.

The last known radio reply was: “We are holding our own.” Soon afterward, the Fitzgerald disappeared. No distress call was heard. The Anderson reported the loss and turned back into the storm to help search. All 29 people aboard died.

Searchers later found the wreck about 160 meters below the surface, in two main sections. The U.S. Coast Guard concluded that water probably entered gradually through hatch covers that were not sufficiently watertight. The National Transportation Safety Board proposed a different final sequence: one or more hatch covers may have failed under the water’s pressure, flooding the hold rapidly. These are investigation conclusions; the final minutes were never fully reconstructed.

snippet.title: How France Used the Eiffel Tower for Military Radio #EiffelTower
snippet.description:
What did the Eiffel Tower have to do with French military radio?

Built for the 1889 World's Fair, the Eiffel Tower later carried antennas used for French military radio. Before that, French forts in the east relied on weather-sensitive tethered balloons to raise antennas. In 1909, a permanent military radio station was installed underground beneath the Champ de Mars park, while its antennas stood high on the tower.

snippet.title: A Third Wheel on Every Date #dating #storytime
snippet.description:
In this story, my boyfriend’s best friend comes on every date. For three months, Matt joins us for movies, walks, and shopping. I want time alone with my boyfriend, but every request turns into another reason to feel guilty.

My boyfriend says Matt has lost his mother and has almost no family or support. I even try arranging a double date, but nothing changes. When I finally plan to break up at the park, Matt comes too.

This time, Matt hears the explanation I’ve been given. His mother is alive. He has siblings and a fiancée. After the breakup, he texts me with something else: he’d been told I didn’t want to be alone with my boyfriend and was asking him to join us.

A story about dating, relationship boundaries, and two people being told completely different things. We never find out why my boyfriend did it. All that time, Matt thought he was doing me a favor.

snippet.description:

snippet.description:
Stone tools survived for more than a million years. Almost all the clothes disappeared.

snippet.title: A Diver Reached for a Hand in a Sunken Tugboat. It Grabbed Back. #HarrisonOkene #Jascon4
snippet.description:
Harrison Okene was the cook aboard the tugboat Jascon-4 when it sank off the coast of Nigeria on 26 May 2013, at a depth of about 30 metres. Trapped inside the wreck, he survived for more than 60 hours in an air pocket.

A diver sent to recover bodies reached for a hand — and it grabbed back. Okene was the only survivor among the 12 people aboard; the other 11 crew members died. Divers brought him to the surface in a diving bell before transferring him to a decompression chamber.

snippet.title: They Opened Her Coffin. She Sat Up. #IrishLegends #Shorts
snippet.description:
An Irish legend tells of Margorie McCall, buried after a fever with a valuable ring still on her swollen finger. After the funeral, thieves opened her coffin and tried to take it. When a knife touched her finger, Margorie sat up and screamed, sending them fleeing.

Still in her burial clothes, she walked home with a bleeding hand. Her husband recognized her knock and opened the door. When he saw her, he clutched his chest and died. Margorie later remarried and lived for years. The tale closes with the words, “Lived once, buried twice.”

snippet.title: The German Report That Revealed Brest Fortress’s Defiance
snippet.description:
The German commander who attacked Brest Fortress later acknowledged how costly it was to assault a determined defense. His own report offers a striking view from the other side of the battle.

On June 22, 1941, artillery struck the fortress as German forces advanced into the Soviet Union. Soviet troops fought from isolated positions, struggling with broken communications, wounded comrades and a desperate shortage of water.

By the end of June, organized defense had largely collapsed, but individuals and small groups continued resisting into July. This film follows the defenders’ struggle and examines what the commander’s report can—and cannot—tell us about it.

snippet.title: Voyager 1 Was Still Sending a Signal—So Why Couldn't Earth Read It?
snippet.description:
Voyager 1 was still reaching Earth by radio, but the information coming back could no longer be read. The spacecraft was about 24 billion kilometers away, so every repair attempt meant waiting almost two days for a reply. Engineers traced the problem to damaged memory, moved the needed program into working space, and rewrote its references. First, the spacecraft's systems report became readable. Then science data returned from all four working instruments.

snippet.title: Why England Tried to Hold Down Wages After the Plague
snippet.description:
After the Black Death, labour shortages gave some survivors a chance to seek better wages or another employer. A 1349 ordinance and the 1351 Statute of Labourers sought to control pay and compel work under set conditions. The old order did not simply return, and survival did not mean freedom from poverty or dependence.

snippet.title: Why War Changed the Clocks
snippet.description:
In 1916, Germany adopted daylight saving time nationwide during World War I. The US followed in 1918, repealed it in 1919 despite President Wilson’s veto, and brought it back during World War II in 1942. War accelerated the spread of the idea, but didn't invent it.

snippet.title: Marseille 1720: Life Inside a City Cut Off by Plague
snippet.description:
What happens when plague cuts off a great trading city? In Marseille, hospitals filled, markets fell silent and the streets became part of an overwhelming emergency. Some residents tried to escape; others remained amid illness, fear and restrictions.

Enter Marseille during the epidemic of 1720 and follow the crisis from the first suspicious deaths to the collapse of ordinary services. This is the story of a city whose quarantine system failed to keep the danger outside—and the people who struggled through the consequences.
